words.d: an object in a level that does something when you interact with it: a door, a switch, a moving platform
a mechanic that hurts you, like spikes or a flame jet
an object that sits still until you interact with it, like a crate or a statue
the match-3 word for an obstacle on the board, like ice or a crate
the absorbed feeling between boredom and frustration, where time disappears
a saved spot where you restart after failing
a small, simple game inside a bigger one

lessons.title: Four kinds of stuff fill a level

cards.text: An empty level is just a hallway. **Walking is not gameplay.** Fill levels with four kinds of stuff: **mechanics, hazards, props and puzzles.**

- **Mechanics:** objects that do something when you use them (doors, switches, moving platforms).
- **Hazards:** mechanics that hurt you.
- **Props:** objects that sit still until you touch them.
- **Puzzles:** challenges with a right answer.
A match-3 board is mostly mechanics and hazards (the blockers) plus a puzzle (the level goal). A merge board adds props: decorations you place and enjoy.
Note: "mechanics" means different things to different designers. Board-game designers mean rule systems, like turns or dice. In this chapter, a mechanic is an object you interact with.

check.q: A block of ice on a match-3 board that you must clear is a…
options: Hazard (a blocker)
Prop (decoration)
Checkpoint (a save)
check.why: It's an obstacle that gets in your way, which is the hazard role in match-3.

cards.text: Even a door is a design decision. **How the player opens it should match the character**, and the method should **stay the same for the whole game.**
A brute kicks doors open. A spy opens them carefully. A soldier blows them up. A locked door must show instantly **why** you can't pass: a huge lock, solid metal, immovable rubble.
A lone lever in an empty room screams "video game". When did you last pull a lever? Keep switches simple and realistic, so cause and effect are easy to read.
In mobile games, locked doors become "unlocks at level X" or a key you collect. The rule is the same: the player must instantly see why it's locked and what opens it.
Doors, levers, cranks: three ways a level says "not yet".

check.q: What must a locked door make clear?
options: Why you can't pass right now
Nothing: let players guess
That it will never open
check.why: An unclear lock just frustrates. A clear one gives the player a goal.

lessons.title: Hazards must look dangerous and be fair

cards.text: A **hazard** is a mechanic that hurts. Unlike enemies, hazards aren't smart. So they **must move in predictable patterns** and **must clearly look dangerous.**
Make danger obvious with every tool: spiky or flaming shapes, warning colours, sounds and particles. Match hazards to the level's theme, like lava in a volcano and falling icicles on a mountain.

**Instant death that comes out of nowhere is cheap.** If a player dies, it should be because they weren't paying attention or mistimed it. Rogers calls the unfair kind "dropping rocks on the player's head".

Rocks on the head in F2P:
- a match-3 board you can't win, however you play
- a runner obstacle you can't see in time
- a surprise that fails the level with no warning
Every unfair loss is a reason to quit.
If players die, they should blame their thumbs, not your name in the credits.

check.q: When is a hazard death fair?
options: When the player could see it coming and mistimed it
When it's a surprise with no warning
When it's random
check.why: Fair deaths come from the player's own mistake, so they want to try again.

cards.text: **Challenge** builds skill: it puts obstacles in front of you that skill can beat. **Difficulty** just punishes. **Aim for challenge.**
Very hard games make a proud few finish. Challenging games let most players finish and feel smart. Rogers talks about a "fun curve": the point where challenge tips into frustration. Never cross it.
The fix is **ramping**: teach one move, let the player master it, then combine and intensify slowly. Each system builds on the one before.

In F2P, "challenging, not difficult" is a business rule: unfair deaths cost players. And the ethics line: a near-miss from real skill is challenge. A near-miss **engineered** to sell +5 moves is manipulation.

check.q: What's the difference between challenge and difficulty?
options: Challenge can be beaten with skill; difficulty just punishes
There is no real difference; they're two words for one thing
Difficulty is more fun, because players like being punished
check.why: Challenge rewards learning. Difficulty frustrates, and most players quit.

lessons.title: Timing puzzles: wait for it… go!

cards.text: A **timing puzzle** is a hazard that moves, like spinning blades or a flame jet. It creates tension: wait… wait… now! **It only feels fair if the player can read the pattern.**

Four rules:
- a movement pattern the eye can follow
- predictable timing, never random
- a tight but possible safe window, with some extra time at both edges
- **tells**: signs that show when and where it's safe
A flame jet first flickers (warning), then blasts (danger), then smokes (go!). The flicker is the tell. Players learn it after one look.
In runners and hyper-casual games, every obstacle needs a readable tell at phone size. If players can't see the warning on a small screen, the hazard is unfair.
Wait for it… wait for it… go for it!

check.q: Why is random timing bad for a timing puzzle?
options: Players can't learn the pattern
It's too easy
It costs more to build
check.why: Timing puzzles reward learning. Random timing makes success luck, not skill.

lessons.title: Props, breakables and the crate problem

cards.text: **Props** make a level feel like a real place: desks, cars, statues, trees. **Let players interact with them**, and breakable props can drop treasure or open new paths.
To brainstorm props, start with the obvious items for the setting, then branch out. When your list turns silly, you've emptied the well. Rest a day, or research with books, games and films.

In the Lego games, almost everything smashes into studs (the game's money). Smashing junk for loot feels great. But crates are the lazy default. Try a vase, a mailbox, a fish tank or a tiki idol instead.
On mobile, "breakables" are piñatas, gift boxes, gumball machines and mystery eggs. Make each one look different, so opening it feels special.
A crate is the placeholder text of level design.

options: They're a boring, lazy default for breakables
They take too long for artists to build
Players can't tell how to break them
check.why: Crates are everywhere. A themed breakable makes the world feel original.

cards.text: Placing mechanics, hazards and enemies is like **composing music.** Bring in each instrument one at a time, let it be learned, then layer them toward a big finish. Done well, this creates **flow**.

The 7-step recipe:
1. simple movement
2. one mechanic, repeated
3. a second mechanic, then both together
4. a hazard
5. enemies, with room to learn them
6. enemies and hazards together
7. a twist: flip one element to keep players alert
**Flow** is the sweet spot between boredom and frustration. Players get absorbed and lose track of time. It's the goal of good level design.
This is exactly how match-3 levels are built. A new blocker gets a showcase level where it appears almost alone. It shows up a few more times, then combines with older blockers.
Strings, flute, oboe, wolf, drums: move, collect, mechanics, enemies, finale.

check.q: A new blocker first appears in a match-3. What's the best first level for it?
options: A level where it appears almost alone
A level with five other new blockers
The hardest level of the chapter
check.why: Introduce one new thing at a time. Combine it with others only after it's learned.

cards.text: You don't need many mechanics. **Three good ones can make dozens of combinations.** The magic is in how you combine them.
Design enemies and hazards to work together, like peanut butter and chocolate. Then rotate mechanics like baseball pitchers: use one for a while, rest it, bring it back. Overuse kills a mechanic.
A fire pit, a moving obstacle and a spinning blade. On their own they're simple. Combined, they give tense jumps, timing runs and enemy traps.
Good match-3 games don't put every blocker in every level. They rotate a few, so each level has its own personality. Runners rotate obstacle sets by zone.
Rotate mechanics like pitchers. Even your best one gets tired if it plays every inning.

check.q: Why rotate mechanics instead of using all of them everywhere?
options: Each one stays fresh and effective
It saves memory
Players prefer fewer levels
check.why: Overuse makes any mechanic boring. Rotation keeps levels distinct.

lessons.title: Checkpoints: a calm spot to restart

cards.text: **Checkpoints** let players save progress, catch their breath and rethink. They can be visible or invisible, but they must be **safe and automatic.**

Five rules:
- face the player in the direction they're travelling
- never next to a hazard or inside an enemy's range
- restart on the ground, with no long animation
- on flat, even ground
- save automatically, never through a menu
Respawning next to a flame jet and burning before you can move feels cheap. Respawning facing a wall, so you must turn the camera, feels clumsy.

On mobile, the whole app is a checkpoint machine. Calls and notifications interrupt constantly, so save on every action and resume exactly where the player left off. Continues ("Save me") should restart you somewhere safe.

check.q: Where should you never put a checkpoint?
options: Next to a hazard or an enemy
On flat ground
Facing the way forward
check.why: Taking damage right as you respawn is unfair and annoying.

lessons.title: Puzzles: show the door, then the key

cards.text: Rogers' definition: **a puzzle is a challenge with a right answer.** The player must know what they're trying to do and what they'll get. **Show them the door, then send them after the key.**

- Keep pieces simple and few.
- When a piece changes, the player must see it change.
- Always give a clear way to reset.
- One simple action should give a visible result, so the player feels closer.
Avoid weird logic. In Resident Evil 2, you place chess pieces in a panel to open a door in a police station. Why would a police station need chess pieces? Strange logic makes players feel stupid.
The level goal in a puzzle game is the "door": show it before the first move ("Collect 20 red gems"). The player then hunts for the "key": the moves that reach it.
Door first, then key.

check.q: What should a player know before solving a puzzle?
options: The goal and the reward
Nothing: discovery is the fun
Only the reward
check.why: Players need to know what they're trying to do, or they're just guessing.

lessons.title: Four ways to solve, and fair hints

cards.text: Players solve puzzles by **reason, knowledge, skill or luck.** The best puzzles allow all four. And **moving forward is something the player is owed, not a prize they earn.**

Aim for the **"aha!" moment**: the instant the player sees how it fits. After that, doing the solution should be quick. If a player is stuck, keep the stakes low: offer hints, or even the full answer.
In Professor Layton games, hints cost a little: you score fewer points the more hints you use. A small price, never a severe one like losing a life.
Paid hints and skips are fine in F2P if they're the player's choice and the price is mild. Hiding the only way forward behind a big payment is not.
Reason, Knowledge, Skill, Luck: "RKSL", say it like "rascal".

check.q: A player is stuck on a puzzle. What should the game do?
options: Offer hints or the answer at a small price
Take away a life
Lock the game until it's solved
check.why: Progress is owed to the player. Help should cost a little, never a lot.

cards.text: A **minigame** is a small, simple game for variety or to represent an activity. A **microgame** lasts only seconds. Rogers believes almost any activity can become a minigame.

Rules:
- simple controls, one action per button
- short: 5 to 10 minutes, or seconds for a microgame
- gentle difficulty: variety, not torture
- something new at each step, even just new art or music
- a clear way to win
Whack-a-Mole is the last resort. It's reaction only, random, repetitive, needs almost no input, and never ends. Players quit from boredom, not victory.

Minigames are everywhere in mobile:
- ads built on pull-the-pin and pick-a-path puzzles
- event minigames like dice boards and digging
- hyper-casual games are often one microgame stretched into a product
Whack-a-Mole's five sins: reflex-only, random, repetitive, one input, endless.

check.q: Why is Whack-a-Mole a weak design?
options: No decisions, no strategy, no real end
It's far too hard for most players
It needs too many buttons to play
check.why: It relies only on reflexes and randomness, so it gets boring fast.
